newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bardot bares bitter heart in kiss-and-tell memoirs.
newsitem.headline: Bardot bares bitter heart in kiss-and-tell memoirs.

text.p: Former sex symbol Brigitte Bardot published her kiss-and-tell memoirs on Tuesday, baring an embittered heart and clinging to her one surviving passion in an ocean of resentment: animal rights.

In "Initiales B.B.", the French movie star adored by a generation of men around the world describes herself as a naive girl who left home at 16 and was thrown unprepared into a world of glitz that drove her to solitude and attempted suicide.

"I thank those who taught me about life by kicking my ass, who by betraying me and taking advantage of my naivety dragged me to the brink of despair, which I escaped by sheer miracle," she wrote in the foreword.

In a 550-page book compiled over 21 years and published days before her 62nd birthday, Bardot, who now devotes her life to animal welfare, tells of broken marriages, an unwanted son and fleeting lovers.

"That was my life, a succession of scandals, of lovers, of films. Only death could bring me serenity...the return to earth was a nightmare," she wrote at the height of her glory after swallowing sleeping pills and slashing her wrists in one of what she said were "quite a few escape attempts".
The birth of her son Nicolas was an ordeal. Doctors refused her an abortion -- illegal at the time in France -- because she was too well-known, and pregnancy was "a nine-month nightmare".

She shouted at his birth: "I don't give a damn, I don't want to see him again." Bardot was later reconciled with Nicolas, now 36, who lives in Norway with a Norwegian wife. But she cannot understand her two grandchildren, who do not speak French.
Bardot bitches about her jet-set travel. She hated Las Vegas, Acapulco was odourless and tasteless, and Puerto Rico was dirt, poverty and stench. But she loved Mexicans and Brazilians.

In New York, fans mobbed her and tore at her dress, baring her famous breasts, almost blinding her in one eye by with a close camera flash. In Geneva, a prudish crowd pelted her with tomatoes amid cries of "Go back to France, whore".
"I could not take it any more, I hated these shitty trips, these shitty reporters," she wrote.

Bardot made the last of her 46 films at 36 in 1973, declaring the film world to be rotten and retiring as a recluse in the fashionable Riviera resort of Saint Tropez where she says she had to hurl firecrackers to keep hordes of tourists at bay.
She fires barbs all around and bares prejudices about homosexuals and Moslems that have already caused her trouble.
Government ministers are "gatecrashers, jackasses and whippersnappers".

"Almost all men are homos," she said in an interview with the magazine Elle, adding that modern women who had driven them to homosexuality were ending up on their own, dressed as clowns by gay fashion designers who did not like women.

Some figures, however, are spared attack -- like her beloved grandfather, nicknamed "Boom", who told her parents to let her go if she wanted to, saying: "If this girl wants to be a whore, she will be, with or without the cinema".
The late president Charles de Gaulle she calls "almost a father" to the French, and of Picasso, writes: "My God, what a man".
Jean-Marie Le Pen, leader of the far-right anti-immigrant National Front, whom Prime Minister Alain Juppe has described as racist, antisemitic and xenophobic, "is pleasant and learned".
Bardot, who has married Le Pen's friend Bernard d'Ormale, is being sued by the Movement against Racism (MRAP) for saying earlier this year that France was being invaded by Moslems.
Her outburst was in protest at the ritual throat-slitting of sheep for the Aid-el-Kebir Moslem feast.

Her love goes above all to animals, and her memoirs tell of her sheep Nenette, her duckling, donkey Cadichon, goat Colinette, dogs Kapi, Clown, Pichnou and her beloved dog Guapa whose death "ended a 15-year love story".
Her famous curves "slack a bit on all sides", but she will not have plastic surgery, she says, explaining: "Animals couldn't care less".

The memoirs end in 1973, the year she quit cinema. She has promised a second volume to tell of her second life, a life "that allows me to bear existing by putting myself to the service of an immense misery, animal misery," she said.
